articles.title: Taxonomic Debate: One Species, Multiple Lineages
articles.summary: Separate formal botanical taxonomy from ancestry, population structure, pedigree, morphology, chemotype, and retail labels.
articles.learningObjective: Explain how one accepted species-level name can coexist with meaningful genetic population structure, historical lineages, admixture, hybridization, and cultivated diversity.
terms: Taxonomy
The scientific practice of naming, describing, and classifying organisms.
Population structure
Non-random genetic differentiation among sampled groups within a species.
Genetic cluster
A grouping inferred from a stated dataset, marker system, sampling plan, and analytical model; it is not automatically a formal taxon.
Admixture
Ancestry derived from previously differentiated populations.
Introgression
Movement of genetic material from one population into another through crossing followed by subsequent reproduction.
Landrace
A historically cultivated, locally adapted population whose claim requires geographic and cultural provenance rather than appearance or marketing alone.
coreScience: The encyclopedia uses Cannabis sativa L. as its controlled species-level baseline under the stated taxonomic authority. That naming decision does not imply genetic uniformity. Species-level naming and within-species diversity answer different biological questions.

Population-genetic and genomic studies have detected meaningful differentiation, admixture, introgression, hybridization, and extensive internal diversity within Cannabis sativa. The exact clusters recovered depend on sampling, provenance, marker choice, reference material, data quality, and analytical model.

Historical terms such as sativa, indica, ruderalis, hemp, drug type, and hybrid have been used as scientific names, geographic or ancestry claims, morphology labels, production categories, flowering shorthand, retail labels, and marketing language. A controlled record therefore preserves what a label was intended to mean instead of treating it as a universal biological category.
Breeding compatibility, morphology, chemotype, pedigree, population ancestry, and legal classification are related layers of evidence, but none can replace all the others.
cultivationRelevance: Do not set irrigation, nutrition, lighting, training, flowering duration, disease expectations, or harvest decisions from sativa, indica, ruderalis, or hybrid labels alone.
For breeding and crop comparison, preserve population size, generation, parent identity, source continuity, and the distinction between seed-derived siblings and clonal material.
When same-labeled plants behave differently, first verify identity, developmental stage, environment, root health, pathogen status, and normal segregation before assigning the difference to ancestry.
measureAndRecord: Accepted botanical name, authority, and review date.
Exact wording from breeder, vendor, package, donor, or prior record.
Whether the label was intended as taxonomy, ancestry, morphology, flowering behavior, production type, effect label, or something else.
Source, custody, dates, accession or lot identifiers, and geographic history when documented.
Marker or genome method, laboratory, sample ID, reference set, result, and limitations.
Observed flowering behavior and measured traits with stage, position, units, and environmental context.
What is established, probable, supplied but unverified, conflicting, or unknown.
misconceptions: One accepted species means all cannabis is genetically the same.
Species-level identity and within-species diversity are different biological levels.
Every genetic cluster is a species.
Clusters are conditional on the sampled material and analysis and do not by themselves establish formal rank.
Broad leaves prove indica ancestry.
Leaf form is influenced by genetics, stage, environment, and selection and cannot independently verify ancestry.
Day-neutral flowering alone proves ruderalis identity.
Record the trait and the pedigree evidence separately; the trait alone does not prove a taxonomic or geographic label.
articles.evidenceLimits: The controlled one-species baseline is a stated nomenclatural framework, not proof that every taxonomist agrees. Population and domestication studies remain sensitive to accession provenance, geographic sampling, unsampled diversity, markers, reference quality, and model assumptions.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online: Cannabis records.
Sawler J. et al. (2015), The Genetic Structure of Marijuana and Hemp, PLOS ONE 10(8):e0133292.
Ren G. et al. (2021), Large-scale whole-genome resequencing unravels the domestication history of Cannabis sativa, Science Advances 7(29):eabg2286.
Grassa C.J. et al. (2021), A new Cannabis genome assembly associates elevated cannabidiol with hemp introgressed into marijuana, New Phytologist 230:1665–1679.
Lynch R.C. et al. (2025), Domesticated cannabinoid synthases amid a wild mosaic cannabis pangenome, Nature 643:1001–1010.

articles.title: Annual Growth Habit and the Whole-Plant Life Cycle
articles.summary: Follow cannabis development by biological stage instead of treating calendar week numbers as universal deadlines.
articles.learningObjective: Describe the major stages of the cannabis life cycle and distinguish developmental stage from time since planting.
terms: Annual
A plant that normally completes germination, reproduction, and senescence within one growing cycle.
Vegetative phase
Development dominated by roots, stems, leaves, and branch architecture.
Reproductive phase
Development of flowers, pollen, fertilization, seed, or mature seedless inflorescences.
Senescence
Regulated aging and remobilization that precedes tissue death.
coreScience: A seed-derived cannabis plant passes through imbibition and germination, seedling establishment, vegetative growth, reproductive transition, flowering, and senescence. If pollination occurs, fertilization and achene development become part of the reproductive sequence.

Clones enter development differently because they begin as already-developed shoot tissue rather than as embryos. Their establishment history therefore cannot be interpreted exactly like a seedling timeline.

Developmental stage is not identical to time since planting. Genetics, temperature, light, root-zone conditions, water status, health, photoperiod, container restriction, and stress can accelerate, delay, or distort visible development.
Photoperiod-responsive and day-neutral material differ in how reproduction is initiated, but onset and duration still vary within those broad categories.
cultivationRelevance: Use calendar age for scheduling and stage observations for biological interpretation.
Record visible milestones such as true-leaf development, node count, preflowers, first visible flowers, pollen shed, and seed maturity instead of relying on a single week label.
Light, irrigation, nutrition, humidity risk, training tolerance, scouting emphasis, and sampling priorities all change with development.
measureAndRecord: First true leaves, rooted cutting, and transplant dates.
Node count, height, branch count, and canopy size.
Preflower, induction, first visible flowers, anthesis, pollination, or seed-development milestones.
Defined observations, harvest date, seed maturity, and tissue decline.
misconceptions: Every plant follows the same week-by-week chart.
Calendars organize work but do not replace stage observations.
Clones are biologically the same age as new seedlings.
A cutting begins as developed donor shoot tissue and carries a different developmental history.
Senescence is always a nutrient deficiency.
Senescence is regulated, although stress and root-zone problems can accelerate or mimic it.
articles.evidenceLimits: The life-cycle framework transfers broadly, but exact stage duration is genotype- and environment-dependent. Fixed-day schedules should be treated as planning aids rather than universal plant biology.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Cannabis sativa L., Plants of the World Online.
Caplan D. et al. (2018), Vegetative propagation of cannabis by stem cuttings, Canadian Journal of Plant Science 98:1126–1132.
Hesami M. et al. (2023), Effect of explant source on phenotypic changes of in vitro grown cannabis plantlets over multiple subcultures, Biology 12:443.
Hesami M., Pepe M., and Jones A.M.P. (2023), Morphological Characterization of Cannabis sativa L. Throughout Its Complete Life Cycle, Plants 12(20):3646.

articles.title: The Cannabis Achene: What Growers Call a Seed
articles.summary: Understand the planted cannabis unit as a dry one-seeded fruit and separate fruit-wall anatomy from the true seed and embryo.
articles.learningObjective: Identify the commercial cannabis 'seed' as an achene and explain why the distinction matters for anatomy, storage, and viability testing.
terms: Achene
A dry, indehiscent, one-seeded fruit whose fruit wall does not open at maturity.
Pericarp
The mature ovary wall that forms the fruit wall.
Seed coat
Protective tissue derived from the ovule integuments around the embryo.
Indehiscent
Not naturally splitting open to release the seed at maturity.
coreScience: The object sold and planted as a cannabis seed is botanically an achene: a small, dry, indehiscent fruit containing one true seed. Everyday cultivation can still use the word seed, but anatomy lessons must distinguish the outer fruit wall from the seed tissues inside.
Inside are the seed coat, limited peripheral endosperm, and embryo. The embryo contains cotyledons, a radicle, a hypocotyl region, and the shoot-apex or plumule region.

Size, color, striping, and firmness can support physical inspection, but they do not prove germination capacity, sex, chemotype, or genetic purity. Viability is physiological and is better assessed with representative testing than appearance alone.
cultivationRelevance: Preserve seed-lot identity, source, generation, harvest year, and storage history as biological inventory data.
Avoid crushing, moisture cycling, and selective testing of only the largest or darkest achenes.
Accurate educational diagrams should separately label fruit wall, seed coat, cotyledons, radicle, hypocotyl, and shoot region.
measureAndRecord: Source, cross or cultivar, generation, harvest year, and quantity.
Cracked, crushed, malformed, discolored, or apparently intact.
Temperature, moisture-control method, container, and duration when known.
Representative sample size and selection method.
Normal germination, abnormal seedling, hard or ungerminated, and dead.
misconceptions: Dark striped seeds are always viable.
Color and mottling vary and do not replace testing.
Large seeds produce female plants.
Achene size does not establish sex.
The outer shell is only a seed coat.
The planted unit also includes the fruit wall.
articles.evidenceLimits: The achene distinction is essential for botanical anatomy, but ordinary cultivation language can still use 'seed' when the anatomical distinction is not material to the decision.
sources: Mangeot-Peter L. et al. (2023), Development and anatomy of hemp achenes, AoB PLANTS 15(6):plad082.
Geneve R.L. et al. (2022), Temperature Limits for Seed Germination in Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.), Crops 2(4):415–427.

articles.title: Embryo, Cotyledons, Radicle, Hypocotyl, and Plumule
articles.summary: Trace the embryonic structures that become the seedling root and shoot system during germination and emergence.
articles.learningObjective: Identify the major cannabis embryo structures and follow their roles through radicle emergence, hypocotyl extension, cotyledon opening, and first true-leaf development.
terms: Embryo
The young sporophyte contained within the seed.
Cotyledon
An embryonic leaf that stores or transfers reserves and becomes photosynthetic after emergence.
Radicle
The embryonic root that normally emerges first during germination.
Hypocotyl
The embryonic stem region below the cotyledons.
Plumule
The embryonic shoot region containing the shoot apex and earliest leaf primordia.
coreScience: The cannabis embryo is a compact plant body prepared to resume growth when water, temperature, oxygen, and viability permit. Radicle emergence marks the first obvious extension of the new root axis.
The hypocotyl elongates during emergence and helps raise the cotyledons. The cotyledons open above the medium and can become photosynthetic while the first true leaves expand.

The shoot apex between the cotyledons produces subsequent leaves and stem nodes. Root injury, hypocotyl constriction, retained coverings, oxygen depletion, salinity, and disease can all interfere with establishment, but they require their own evidence rather than diagnosis from one stalled seedling.
cultivationRelevance: Avoid unnecessary handling of an exposed radicle; long exposed radicles are particularly easy to damage.
Score seedling establishment by structure: radicle, hypocotyl, cotyledons, shoot apex, first true leaves, and root-shoot balance.
Breaking the surface does not by itself prove a normal seedling.
measureAndRecord: Date/time from start and approximate length when useful.
Upright, stretched, constricted, discolored, or damaged.
Opened, green, damaged, retained covering, or abnormal.
Date visible and symmetry or distortion.
Normal, weak root, weak shoot, or both abnormal.
misconceptions: The first two round leaves are true leaves.
They are cotyledons, which have a different developmental origin.
The emerging radicle should be green.
It is embryonic root tissue and is typically pale before light exposure.
A seedling that breaks the surface has passed.
Normal development requires coordinated roots, hypocotyl, cotyledons, and shoot apex.
articles.evidenceLimits: Exact emergence timing depends on seed lot, temperature, moisture, oxygen, and method. The structural sequence is more transferable than a fixed hour count.
sources: Mangeot-Peter L. et al. (2023), Development and anatomy of hemp achenes, AoB PLANTS 15(6):plad082.
Geneve R.L. et al. (2022), Temperature Limits for Seed Germination in Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.), Crops 2(4):415–427.
Muthert L.W.F. et al. (2020), Root Tropisms, Frontiers in Plant Science 10:1807.
Pan J. et al. (2021), Mechanisms of Waterlogging Tolerance in Plants, Frontiers in Plant Science 11:627331.

articles.title: Root System Architecture
articles.summary: Understand the primary root, lateral roots, fine roots, root hairs, and root-zone conditions that shape a changing absorption system.
articles.learningObjective: Describe how the initial root axis develops into a distributed absorption and transport system and connect root architecture to water, oxygen, media, and diagnostic observations.
terms: Primary root
The root axis derived from the radicle.
Lateral root
A branch root initiated from internal root tissues.
Root hair
A short-lived epidermal extension that increases contact with water and ions.
Rhizosphere
The zone of soil or substrate influenced by roots and their exudates.
coreScience: A seed-derived cannabis plant begins with a primary root derived from the radicle. Lateral roots expand from that axis and produce finer absorbing roots. In containers, transplanting, pruning, water placement, oxygen distribution, and physical barriers can substantially alter mature architecture.

The growing root tip includes a root cap and apical meristem followed by zones of cell division, elongation, and differentiation. Root hairs form behind the tip and increase contact with surrounding solution and particles.

Living roots require oxygen for aerobic respiration. Waterlogged pore space can reduce oxygen availability, energy supply, and root function. Compaction, salinity, temperature, and pathogens can also injure roots and can create above-ground symptoms that resemble nutrient or water problems.
cultivationRelevance: Irrigation should wet the intended root zone without maintaining prolonged oxygen deprivation.
Repeatedly wetting only a small pocket can limit root exploration, while persistent saturation can also impair function.
During transplant or diagnostic sampling, record distribution, firmness, new tips, discoloration, odor, lesions, and sloughing; no single root color proves disease.
measureAndRecord: Container, bed, field, water culture, slab, or other system.
Moisture distribution, compaction, drainage, and air space.
Surface, edge, bottom, uniform, circling, sparse, or localized.
New tips, firmness, discoloration, odor, lesions, or sloughing.
Root-zone temperature, moisture, pH, EC, and irrigation history.
misconceptions: More water always means more uptake.
Uptake requires functional living roots, oxygen, favorable water potential, and intact transport.
White roots prove perfect health.
Color is useful but not definitive and can be affected by media and staining.
A large container automatically creates a large root system.
Roots expand only where physical, chemical, and biological conditions support growth.
articles.evidenceLimits: Direct cannabis root research is less abundant than shoot and flower research. General root physiology is applicable, while system-specific targets require direct validation.
sources: Hesami M., Pepe M., and Jones A.M.P. (2023), Morphological Characterization of Cannabis sativa L. Throughout Its Complete Life Cycle, Plants 12(20):3646.
Pan J. et al. (2021), Mechanisms of Waterlogging Tolerance in Plants: Research Progress and Prospects, Frontiers in Plant Science 11:627331.

articles.title: Stem Anatomy and Vascular Transport
articles.summary: Connect cannabis stem tissues to mechanical support and the movement of water, minerals, sugars, and signals through the plant.
articles.learningObjective: Identify major stem tissues and explain how xylem, phloem, cambium, and structural tissues support transport and canopy load.
terms: Xylem
Vascular tissue conducting water and dissolved minerals primarily from roots toward shoots.
Phloem
Vascular tissue distributing sugars and other transported compounds between sources and sinks.
Cambium
A lateral meristem that contributes to secondary vascular growth.
Pith
Central stem tissue that can contribute to storage and internal structure.
coreScience: The cannabis stem is both a support column and a transport network. Young stems contain outer epidermal and cortical tissues, vascular bundles, cambial regions, and central pith. Xylem lies primarily toward the interior of vascular tissue and phloem toward the exterior.

Xylem flow is driven largely by water-potential gradients associated with transpiration and depends on root supply and intact conducting tissue. Phloem distributes photosynthates and other compounds between source tissues and sinks such as growing shoots, roots, and flowers.

Bending or cutting changes mechanical loading and vascular continuity. Plants can reinforce injured areas through wound responses, but severe crushing, splitting, girdling, constriction, infection, or repeated movement can compromise transport.
cultivationRelevance: Support decisions should account for increasing flower mass and lever forces rather than using stem diameter as the only indicator of branch-failure risk.
When one branch wilts while the rest of the plant remains normal, inspect the stem and branch junction for a localized kink, girdle, lesion, or break before assuming a whole-root-zone problem.
Document injury location and recovery rather than treating a healed-looking knuckle as proof of full vascular or structural recovery.
measureAndRecord: Angle, included bark or crease, splitting, and support.
Location, length, depth, discoloration, and date.
Whole plant, one branch, or tissue above an injury.
New growth, wound tissue, continued wilt, or failure.
misconceptions: Xylem pumps water.
Water movement depends largely on physical gradients and transpiration, supported by living root processes.
A healed-looking knuckle is always stronger.
Appearance does not prove restored transport or resistance to future load.
Purple stems prove phosphorus deficiency.
Pigmentation can reflect genetics, light, temperature, age, or stress and is not diagnostic alone.
articles.evidenceLimits: Detailed stem anatomy varies with age, position, cultivar, and breeding history. The tissue functions described here are a transferable baseline, not a universal mechanical threshold.
sources: Hesami M., Pepe M., and Jones A.M.P. (2023), Morphological Characterization of Cannabis sativa L. Throughout Its Complete Life Cycle, Plants 12(20):3646.
Savatin D.V. et al. (2014), Wounding in the plant tissue: the defense of a dangerous passage, Frontiers in Plant Science 5:470.

articles.title: Nodes, Internodes, and Branch Attachment
articles.summary: Use nodes, internodes, and branch order as repeatable plant-architecture measurements rather than vague descriptors.
articles.learningObjective: Distinguish nodes from internodes, measure their development consistently, and connect branch attachment to canopy architecture and structural loading.
terms: Node
A stem position where leaves, axillary buds, branches, or flowers attach.
Internode
The stem segment between two nodes.
Axillary bud
A bud formed in the angle between a leaf and stem.
Branch order
A hierarchical description of main stem, primary branch, secondary branch, and later branches.
coreScience: Nodes are repeated developmental units that can bear leaves and axillary meristems. Internodes separate those units and contribute strongly to plant height and canopy openness.

Node number and internode length answer different questions. A tall plant can have many nodes, long internodes, or both. Internode length reflects genetics, developmental stage, light environment, temperature relationships, competition, hormones, root conditions, and stress.

Branch attachments carry increasing loads as shoots elongate and flowers develop. Attachment geometry, tissue development, previous injury, support, and uneven loading can affect failure risk, but there is no single universal cannabis branch-angle threshold.
cultivationRelevance: Use a written node-count rule and state whether cotyledon nodes or incomplete nodes are excluded.
Measure comparable internode positions rather than selecting only the longest segment.
Treat the node as a useful observation site for architecture, axillary growth, preflowers, and reproductive development.
measureAndRecord: What counts and what is excluded.
Weak angle, split, load, support, or no concern.
misconceptions: Long internodes always mean low light.
Light is one possible cause among several interacting variables.
More nodes always mean more yield.
Yield depends on source, sink, health, environment, and management factors beyond node count.
Every bump on a stem is a node.
A node is a repeated organ-attachment position, not any surface feature.
articles.evidenceLimits: Architecture measurements become useful only when definitions, positions, units, developmental stage, and comparison conditions are consistent.
sources: Hesami M., Pepe M., and Jones A.M.P. (2023), Morphological Characterization of Cannabis sativa L. Throughout Its Complete Life Cycle, Plants 12(20):3646.
Onoda Y. and Anten N.P.R. (2011), Challenges to understand plant responses to wind, Plant Signaling & Behavior 6(7):1057–1059.
